claim: FAK inhibitors are currently undergoing clinical testing in combination with anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) inhibitors are currently undergoing clinical testing in combination with anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a factual statement about ongoing clinical trials.

claim: Cancer cell expression of CD80 sensitizes murine tumors to a FAK inhibitor.
source: We identify that cancer cell expression of the T-cell co-stimulatory ligand CD80 sensitizes murine tumors to a FAK inhibitor
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing tumor responses in CD80+ vs CD80- cell lines.

claim: Targeting OX-40 and 4-1BB in combination with FAK can drive enhanced anti-tumor immunity and complete regression of murine tumors.
source: In the absence of CD80, we identify that targeting alternative T-cell co-stimulatory receptors, in particular OX-40 and 4-1BB in combination with FAK, can drive enhanced anti-tumor immunity and even complete regression of murine tumors.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5 demonstrating complete regression with these combinations.

claim: FAK is a non-receptor protein tyrosine kinase that plays a pleotropic role in regulating cancer development and progression.
source: Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) is a non-receptor protein tyrosine kinase that plays a pleotropic role in regulating cancer development and progression.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: FAK was initially identified as a protein highly phosphorylated in response to integrin activation and primarily located at focal adhesions.
source: Initially identified as a protein highly phosphorylated in response to integrin activation and primarily located at cell–extracellular matrix adhesion sites termed focal adhesions
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about FAK's initial characterization.

claim: FAK regulates cellular processes including migration, invasion, adhesion, polarity, proliferation, and survival.
source: FAK is now known to regulate a number of cellular processes linked to the malignant phenotype including migration, invasion, adhesion, polarity, proliferation, and survival (McLean et al., 2005; Sulzmaier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: FAK can translocate to the nucleus of cancer cells where it regulates inflammatory gene expression programs.
source: Furthermore, FAK can also translocate to the nucleus of cancer cells where it regulates inflammatory gene expression programs (Lim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2012.

claim: FAK regulates chemokines and cytokines that orchestrate the composition of tumor microenvironment, promoting immune evasion and resistance to immunotherapy.
source: This includes chemokines and cytokines, which orchestrate the composition of tumor microenvironment (TME), promoting immune evasion and resistance to immunotherapy at least in some scenarios (Jiang et al., 2016; Serrels et al., 2015; Serrels et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FAK kinase inhibitors are generally well tolerated in Phase-I clinical trials.
source: A number of small molecule FAK kinase inhibitors have now either completed, or are currently in, Phase-I clinical trials and results thus far suggest that they are generally well tolerated (de Jonge et al., 2019; Doi et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2015; Soria et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical trial reports.

claim: Loss of expression of Merlin and/or E-cadherin have been suggested as potential markers of sensitivity to FAK inhibitors.
source: Loss of expression of the tumor suppressor protein Merlin (also known as Neurofibromin 2) and/or E-cadherin have both been suggested as potential markers of sensitivity to FAK inhibitors (Hirt et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2017; Shah et al., 2014; Shapiro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A clinical trial testing Merlin as a predictive marker for sensitivity to the FAK inhibitor Defactinib did not prove successful.
source: However, a clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01870609) testing Merlin as a predictive marker for sensitivity to the FAK inhibitor Defactinib did not prove successful.
evidence: This is supported by reference to a specific clinical trial.

claim: FAK knockout or the FAK kinase inhibitor VS-4718 can drive complete CD8 T-cell dependent regression of established SCC tumors.
source: These trials stem from our previous work showing that FAK knockout or the FAK kinase inhibitor VS-4718 can drive complete CD8 T-cell dependent regression of established SCC tumors through shifting the balance of CD8 T-cells: Regulatory T-cells (Tregs) in favor of tumor clearance (Serrels et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: VS-4718 can drive reprogramming of the immuno-suppressive pancreatic TME, including a reduction in Tregs, CD206+ macrophages, MDSCs, and stromal fibroblasts.
source: and that of others showing that VS-4718 can drive reprogramming of the immuno-suppressive pancreatic TME, including a reduction in Tregs, CD206+ macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and stromal fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to work by others.

claim: VS-4718 renders pancreatic tumors responsive to the combination of dual immune checkpoint therapy and chemotherapy (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4, and Gemcitabine).
source: This renders pancreatic tumors responsive to the combination of dual immune checkpoint therapy and chemotherapy (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4, and Gemcitabine) (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: Daily treatment of SCC FAK-wt tumors with 50 mg/kg BI 853520 resulted in complete tumor regression with similar kinetics to that of SCC FAK-/- tumors.
source: Daily treatment of SCC FAK-wt tumors with 50 mg/kg BI 853520 resulted in complete tumor regression with similar kinetics to that of SCC FAK-/-tumors (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Treatment of SCC FAK-/- tumors with BI 853520 had no effect on tumor growth.
source: Treatment of SCC FAK-/-tumors with BI 853520 had no effect on tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: BI 853520 treatment results in complete regression of SCC7.1 tumors by day 27.
source: We observed complete regression of SCC7.1 tumors by day 27 (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SCC6.2 tumors exhibit only a modest growth delay in response to BI 853520.
source: while in contrast a different SCC cell line, SCC6.2, tumors exhibited only a modest growth delay (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Met01 tumors show a heterogeneous response to BI 853520, with 3 out of 10 tumors showing only a growth delay and 7 out of 10 tumors displaying stable disease.
source: Subcutaneous injection of Met01 cells into FVB/N mice followed by daily treatment with either Vehicle or BI 853520 identified a heterogeneous response to BI 853520, with 3 out of 10 tumors showing only a growth delay and 7 out of 10 tumors displaying stable disease for the duration of the study (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Panc43 tumors exhibit only a modest growth delay in response to FAK inhibition.
source: subcutaneous injection of Panc43, Panc47, or Panc117 cells into C57BL/6 mice followed by daily treatment with either Vehicle or BI 853520 identified that Panc43 tumors exhibit only a modest growth delay in response to FAK inhibition (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Panc47 and Panc117 tumors exhibit no response to BI 853520.
source: while Panc47 and Panc117 tumors exhibit no response (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: SCC7.1 tumor regression in response to BI 853520 is CD8 T-cell dependent.
source: In mice treated with a CD8 T-cell depleting antibody, SCC7.1 and Met01 tumors exhibited only a modest growth delay in response to treatment with BI 853520 when compared to Vehicle treated controls, while in mice treated with an isotype control antibody all SCC7.1 tumors underwent complete regression and all Met01 tumors exhibited stable disease following treatment with BI 853520 (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by CD8 T-cell depletion experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Met01 stable disease in response to BI 853520 is CD8 T-cell dependent.
source: In mice treated with a CD8 T-cell depleting antibody, SCC7.1 and Met01 tumors exhibited only a modest growth delay in response to treatment with BI 853520 when compared to Vehicle treated controls, while in mice treated with an isotype control antibody all SCC7.1 tumors underwent complete regression and all Met01 tumors exhibited stable disease following treatment with BI 853520 (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by CD8 T-cell depletion experiments shown in Figure 1I.

claim: FAK kinase inhibition acts via CD8 T-cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity to induce SCC7.1 tumor regression and Met01 stable disease.
source: Thus, FAK kinase inhibition acts via CD8 T-cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity to induce SCC7.1 tumor regression and Met01 stable disease.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CD8 T-cell depletion experiments.

claim: SCC7.1 and Met01 tumors have a higher frequency of CD8 T-cell infiltration than SCC6.2, Panc43 and Panc47 tumors.
source: This identified that SCC7.1 and Met01 tumors have a higher frequency of CD8 T-cell infiltration than SCC6.2, Panc43 and Panc47 tumors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Panc117 tumors have a higher frequency of CD8 T-cell infiltration when compared to SCC6.2, Panc43, and Panc47 tumors.
source: However, Panc117 tumors also had a higher frequency of CD8 T-cell infiltration when compared to SCC6.2, Panc43, and Panc47 tumors.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD8 T-cell infiltration alone does not accurately predict response to BI 853520.
source: Therefore, CD8 T-cell infiltration alone does not accurately predict response to BI 853520.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Panc117 has high CD8 infiltration but does not respond to BI 853520.

claim: The immune checkpoint receptor PD-1 is expressed on activated (CD44+) CD8 T-cells in all tumor types tested.
source: Initially, we used flow cytometry to show that the immune checkpoint receptor Programmed Death Receptor 1 (PD-1) was expressed on activated (CD44+) CD8 T-cells in all tumor types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: None of the cell lines expressed PD-L1 or PD-L2 under basal culture conditions.
source: We next showed that none of the cell lines expressed PD-L1 or PD-L2 under basal culture conditions (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though data not shown.

claim: All cell lines upregulated PD-L1 to a similar extent when stimulated with 10 ng/ml IFNγ for 24 hr.
source: However, when the cell lines were stimulated with 10 ng/ml interferon-gamma (IFNγ) for 24 hr all cell lines upregulated PD-L1 to a similar extent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: None of the cell lines upregulated the expression of PD-L2 in response to IFNγ treatment.
source: None of the cell lines upregulated the expression of PD-L2 in response to IFNγ treatment (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though data not shown.

claim: CD80 is expressed exclusively by the SCC7.1 and Met01 cell lines that respond best to FAK inhibition.
source: We therefore profiled the expression of the B7 family of proteins across the tumor cell lines. While many of these ligands were not expressed by any of the cell lines, CD80 (also known as B7.1) was expressed exclusively by the SCC7.1 and Met01 cell lines that respond best to FAK inhibition (Figure 2A,B), thus correlating with response to BI 853520.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: CD80 is a ligand for two receptors, CTLA-4 and CD28.
source: CD80 is a ligand for two receptors, CTLA-4 and CD28 (Linsley et al., 1991; Linsley et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CTLA-4 is a co-inhibitory receptor associated with suppression of anti-tumor immune responses.
source: CTLA-4 is a co-inhibitory receptor associated with suppression of anti-tumor immune responses and has a higher affinity than CD28 for binding CD80 (van der Merwe et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CTLA-4 has a higher affinity than CD28 for binding CD80.
source: CTLA-4 is a co-inhibitory receptor associated with suppression of anti-tumor immune responses and has a higher affinity than CD28 for binding CD80 (van der Merwe et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CTLA-4 can deplete CD80 from the surface of neighboring cells through the process of trans-endocytosis.
source: Through the process of trans-endocytosis CTLA-4 can deplete CD80 from the surface of neighboring cells (Qureshi et al., 2011), preventing CD80 - CD28 interaction and resulting T-cell co-stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Qureshi et al., 2011.

claim: Regulatory T-cells represent a major cellular source of CTLA-4.
source: Regulatory T-cells, which we have previously shown are depleted from the tumor environment in response to treatment with a FAK inhibitor (Serrels et al., 2015), represent a major cellular source of CTLA-4 (Walker and Sansom, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Treatment with BI 853520 results in a significant decrease in CTLA-4+ immune cells in SCC7.1 tumors.
source: Treatment with BI 853520 resulted in a significant decrease in CTLA-4+ immune cells (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Treatment with BI 853520 results in an increase in the frequency of CD45- cells expressing CD80 on their cell surface in SCC7.1 tumors.
source: and an increase in the frequency of CD45- cells expressing CD80 on their cell surface (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment with a FAK inhibitor shifts the balance in favor of CD80 - CD28 interaction and T-cell co-stimulation.
source: Therefore, treatment with a FAK inhibitor shifts the balance in favor of CD80 - CD28 interaction and T-cell co-stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed changes in CTLA-4 and CD80 expression.

claim: Both CD80 and CD28 blockade significantly impaired the anti-tumor efficacy of BI 853520 in SCC7.1 tumors.
source: Both CD80 and CD28 blockade significantly impaired the anti-tumor efficacy of BI 853520 (Figure 2E), implying an important role for CD80 in regulating response to a FAK inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SCC6.2 cells have a similar expression profile of MHC molecules to that of CD80+ SCC7.1 cells.
source: Using nanostring gene expression analysis we first confirmed that SCC6.2 cells have a similar expression profile of Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules to that of CD80+ SCC7.1 cells that respond to BI 853520 (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is supported by nanostring gene expression data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Expression of CD80 had no impact on SCC6.2 tumor growth in the absence of BI 853520.
source: Expression of CD80 had no impact on SCC6.2 tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: SCC6.2 pcDNA3-CD80 tumors showed a significantly improved response to BI 853520 in comparison to Vehicle treated controls or SCC6.2 pcDNA3 tumors treated with BI 853520.
source: However, SCC6.2 pcDNA3-CD80 tumors showed a significantly improved response to BI 853520 in comparison to either Vehicle treated controls or SCC6.2 pcDNA3 tumors treated with BI 853520.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: CD80 expression sensitizes SCC6.2 tumors to BI 853520.
source: Thus, CD80 expression sensitizes SCC6.2 tumors to BI 853520.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tumor growth experiments with CD80-transfected cells.

claim: Cancer cell expression of CD80, most likely in combination with MHC-I expression, has the potential to identify tumors with increased sensitivity to FAK kinase inhibition.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that cancer cell expression of CD80, most likely in combination with MHC-I expression, has the potential to identify tumors with increased sensitivity to FAK kinase inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective experimental findings.

claim: CD80 expression is upregulated in human colonic epithelial cells isolated from preneoplastic adenomas.
source: Recent studies suggest that CD80 expression is upregulated in human colonic epithelial cells isolated from preneoplastic adenomas (Marchiori et al., 2019; Scarpa et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A population of Cancer Stem Cells (CSCs) that express CD80 have been reported in both murine and human skin SCC tumors.
source: while in skin SCC, a population of Cancer Stem Cells (CSCs) that express CD80 have been reported in both murine and human tumors (Miao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miao et al., 2019.

claim: Murine skin CSCs are identified by expression of Cd34, Itga6, high expression of integrins in general, and responsiveness to TGFβ as indicated by activation of downstream signaling including expression of Cdkn1a.
source: These murine skin CSCs are identified by expression of a number of genes including Cd34, Itga6, high expression of integrins in general, and responsiveness to TGFβ as indicated by activation of downstream signaling including expression of Cdkn1a (Miao et al., 2019; Oshimori et al., 2015; Schober and Fuchs, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CD34+ skin CSCs reside near the tumor vasculature at the tumor stromal interface and express Vegfa.
source: Furthermore, previous related studies have also shown that CD34+ skin CSCs reside near the tumor vasculature at the tumor stromal interface and express Vegfa (Beck et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beck et al., 2011.

claim: SCC7.1 cells express significantly more Cd34 and Itga6 than SCC6.2 cells.
source: Nanostring gene expression analysis and flow cytometry identified that SCC7.1 cells express significantly more Cd34 and Itga6 (Integrin alpha-6) than SCC6.2 cells (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by nanostring and flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: SCC7.1 cells express higher levels of Itga2, Itgb1, Itgb2, Itgb4, Cdkn1a, and Vegfa when compared to SCC6.2 cells.
source: Furthermore, SCC7.1 cells also expressed higher levels of Itga2, Itgb1, Itgb2, Itgb4, Cdkn1a, and Vegfa when compared to SCC6.2 cells (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by nanostring gene expression data shown in Figures 3C-E.

claim: SCC7.1 cells express a gene signature that overlaps with that of CD80+ CSCs previously identified in murine and human SCCs.
source: Thus, SCC7.1 cells express a gene signature that overlaps with that of CD80+ CSCs previously identified in murine and human SCCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the gene expression analysis comparing SCC7.1 to previously reported CSC markers.

claim: CD80 transcript is present in a substantial proportion of cell lines from solid epithelial cancers.
source: This identified that CD80 transcript is present in a substantial proportion of cell lines from solid epithelial cancers, albeit a considerable proportion were also negative for CD80 expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Human Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PTK2 (FAK gene) is highly expressed in all cell lines originating from solid epithelial cancers.
source: PTK2 (FAK gene) was highly expressed in all cell lines originating from solid epithelial cancers (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Human Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Hematological malignancies including lymphomas generally express higher levels of CD80 when compared to cell lines originating from solid epithelial cancers.
source: Interestingly, although perhaps not unexpected, this analysis also identified that hematological malignancies including lymphomas generally expressed higher levels of CD80 when compared to cell lines originating from solid epithelial cancers (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Human Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PTK2 is only expressed in a subset of cell lines from hematological malignancies.
source: PTK2 was only expressed in a subset of cell lines from hematological malignancies (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Human Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-expression of high levels of CD80 and PTK2 transcript occurs preferentially in cancer cell lines originating from patients with Burkitt's Lymphoma, Hodgkin's Lymphoma, Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, and Diffuse Large B-cell (DLBCL) Lymphoma.
source: These analyses suggested that co-expression of high levels of CD80 and PTK2 transcript occurs preferentially in cancer cell lines originating from patients with Burkitt's Lymphoma, Hodgkin's Lymphoma, Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, and Diffuse Large B-cell (DLBCL) Lymphoma.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Human Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: FAK inhibitors have not been tested in patients with Burkitt's Lymphoma, Hodgkin's Lymphoma, Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, and DLBCL.
source: To our knowledge FAK inhibitors have not been tested in patients diagnosed with these cancer types.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge claim about the current state of clinical testing.

claim: CD80-expressing cancer cells are present in some solid epithelial cancers and some blood cancers.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that CD80-expressing cancer cells are present in some solid epithelial cancers and some blood cancers, supporting the potential to select patients based on cancer cell CD80 expression for treatment with a FAK inhibitor.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cell line expression analysis.

claim: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with Vehicle + anti-GITR agonistic antibody resulted in a small growth delay when compared to control treated tumors.
source: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with Vehicle + anti-GITR agonistic antibody resulted in a small growth delay when compared to control treated tumors, which was not improved when the anti-GITR antibody was combined with BI 853520 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Combining anti-GITR with BI 853520 did not improve the response of SCC6.2 tumors compared to anti-GITR alone.
source: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with Vehicle + anti-GITR agonistic antibody resulted in a small growth delay when compared to control treated tumors, which was not improved when the anti-GITR antibody was combined with BI 853520 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with anti-CD40 agonistic antibody alone or in combination with BI 853520 produced similar results to anti-GITR.
source: Similar results were observed using an anti-CD40 agonistic antibody alone or in combination with BI 853520 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with Vehicle + anti-4-1BB agonistic antibody resulted in 2 out of 8 tumors undergoing complete regression and the remaining six tumors exhibiting a delay in growth.
source: However, treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with Vehicle + anti-4-1BB agonistic antibody resulted in 2 out of 8 tumors undergoing complete regression and the remaining six tumors exhibiting a delay in growth when compared to control treated tumors.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Combining anti-4-1BB with BI 853520 resulted in 4 out of 8 tumors undergoing complete regression, and the remaining four tumors exhibiting an improved growth delay.
source: Combining anti-4-1BB with BI 853520 further improved this response, resulting in 4 out of 8 tumors undergoing complete regression, and the remaining four tumors exhibiting an improved growth delay when compared with Vehicle + anti-4-1BB (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with Vehicle + anti-OX40 agonistic antibody resulted in 2 out of 8 tumors undergoing complete regression, and the remaining six exhibiting a growth delay.
source: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with Vehicle + anti-OX40 agonistic antibody resulted in 2 out of 8 tumors undergoing complete regression, and the remaining six exhibiting a growth delay when compared to control treated tumors.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Combining anti-OX40 with BI 853520 resulted in complete regression of all SCC6.2 tumors.
source: Combining anti-OX40 with BI 853520 resulted in complete regression of all tumors (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The FAK kinase inhibitor in combination with activation of either OX40 or 4-1BB represents a potentially promising therapeutic strategy.
source: Thus, the FAK kinase inhibitor in combination with activation of either OX40 or 4-1BB represents a potentially promising therapeutic strategy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tumor growth experiments.

claim: SCC6.2 tumor regression in response to BI 853520 + anti-OX40 is dependent on CD8 T-cells.
source: In mice receiving anti-CD8 antibody the combination of BI 853520 + anti-OX40 resulted in a growth delay when compared to mice treated with anti-CD8 antibody and Vehicle. However, only in mice receiving an isotype control antibody the combination of BI 853520 + anti-OX40 resulted in complete regression of all tumors, implying that tumor regression was dependent on CD8 T-cells.
evidence: This is supported by CD8 T-cell depletion experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SCC6.2 tumor regression in response to BI 853520 + anti-OX40 results in lasting immunological memory that renders mice resistant to further tumor growth.
source: Therefore, SCC6.2 tumor regression in response to BI 853520 + anti-OX40 resulted in lasting immunological memory that renders mice resistant to further tumor growth.
evidence: This is supported by tumor rechallenge experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Both anti-OX40 and BI 853520 treatment result in a reduction in Tregs in SCC6.2 tumors.
source: Both anti-OX40 and BI 853520 treatment resulted in a reduction in Tregs, as did the combination of BI 853520 + anti-OX40 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In tumors treated with anti-OX40 or anti-OX40 + BI 853520, reduction in Tregs was accompanied by an increase in the frequency of non-Treg CD4+ T-cells.
source: In tumors treated with anti-OX40 or anti-OX40 + BI 853520, this was accompanied by an increase in the frequency of non-Treg CD4+ T-cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Treatment with anti-OX40 or BI 853520 + anti-OX40 results in an increase in effector CD8 T-cells (CD8eff) when compared to control treated and BI 853520 treated tumors.
source: Treatment with anti-OX40 or BI 853520 + anti-OX40 also resulted in an increase in effector CD8 T-cells (CD8eff) when compared to control treated and BI 853520 treated tumors (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Anti-OX40 is required to drive increased CD8eff T-cell numbers in SCC6.2 tumors.
source: implying that anti-OX40 is required to drive increased CD8eff T-cell numbers in SCC6.2 tumors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the flow cytometry data.

claim: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with anti-OX40 results in an increase in ICOS expression on both non-Treg CD4 T-cells and CD8eff T-cells.
source: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with anti-OX40 resulted in an increase in ICOS expression on both non-Treg CD4 T-cells and CD8eff T-cells, and this was further increased, especially on CD8eff T-cells, when anti-OX40 was used in combination with BI 853520 (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: ICOS expression on CD8eff T-cells is further increased when anti-OX40 is used in combination with BI 853520.
source: Treatment of SCC6.2 tumors with anti-OX40 resulted in an increase in ICOS expression on both non-Treg CD4 T-cells and CD8eff T-cells, and this was further increased, especially on CD8eff T-cells, when anti-OX40 was used in combination with BI 853520 (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Increased expression of ICOS on CD8eff T-cells is observed in response to BI 853520 treatment in SCC7.1 tumors that express CD80.
source: Interestingly, increased expression of ICOS on CD8eff T-cells was also observed in response to BI 853520 treatment in SCC7.1 tumors that express the co-stimulatory molecule CD80 (Figure 6—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: FAK inhibition may broadly regulate expression of ICOS on CD8 T-cells when a T-cell co-stimulatory signal is present.
source: suggesting that FAK inhibition may more broadly regulate expression of ICOS on CD8 T-cells when a T-cell co-stimulatory signal is present.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of ICOS upregulation in both SCC6.2 and SCC7.1 tumors.

claim: BI 853520 either alone or in combination with OX40 results in a decrease in PD-L2 expression by macrophages in SCC6.2 tumors.
source: Furthermore, we found that macrophage expression of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 and was not altered (Figure 6F), but that BI 853520 either alone or in combination with OX40 resulted in a decrease in PD-L2 expression by macrophages (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Macrophage expression of PD-L1 is not altered by BI 853520 treatment in SCC6.2 tumors.
source: Furthermore, we found that macrophage expression of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 and was not altered (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Macrophages and DCs express the highest levels of PD-L2 among cancer cells, G-MDSCs, M-MDSCs, macrophages, and CD11b+ DCs.
source: Comparison of PD-L2 expression on cancer cells, G-MDSCs, M-MDSCs, macrophages, and CD11b+ DCs revealed that macrophages and DCs express the highest levels of PD-L2 from this range of cell types (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: BI 853520 treatment either alone or in combination with anti-OX40 results in a reduction in PD-L2+ cancer cells and M-MDSCs.
source: BI 853520 treatment either alone or in combination with anti-OX40 also resulted in a reduction in PD-L2+ cancer cells and M-MDSCs (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: BI 853520 treatment generally depletes the availability of PD-L2 within the tumor microenvironment.
source: Therefore, BI 853520 treatment generally depletes the availability of PD-L2 within the tumor microenvironment, likely impacting on decrease of PD-L2-PD-1 signaling and ultimately escape of CD8 T-cells from exhaustion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed reduction in PD-L2 expression across multiple cell types.

claim: BI 853520 treatment results in a small decrease in PD-L2 expression on bone marrow-derived macrophages following stimulation with IL-4 in vitro.
source: BI 853520 treatment resulted in a small decrease in PD-L2 expression following stimulation with IL-4, however this did not appear to fully account for the substantial reduction observed in vivo (Figure 6G) suggesting that FAK-dependent regulation of PD-L2 expression in the TME may be more complex.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: By day 21, 5 out of 10 tumors treated with anti-OX40 + anti-PD-L2 had undergone complete regression, while all tumors treated with anti-OX40 alone were still present.
source: By day 21, 5 out of 10 tumors treated with anti-OX40 + anti-PD-L2 had undergone complete regression, while in contrast all tumors treated with anti-OX40 alone were still present, albeit small.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Anti-PD-L2 in combination with anti-4-1BB resulted in a small decrease in the mean tumor volume at day 21 when compared to anti-4-1BB alone, but this was not statistically significant.
source: Anti-PD-L2 in combination with anti-4-1BB resulted in a small decrease in the mean tumor volume at day 21 when compared to anti-4-1BB alone. However, this was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Regulation of PD-L2 likely contributes more towards the anti-tumor efficacy of BI 853520 when used in combination with anti-OX40.
source: Therefore, regulation of PD-L2 likely contributes more towards the anti-tumor efficacy of BI 853520 when used in combination with anti-OX40.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of anti-PD-L2 with anti-OX40 vs anti-4-1BB.

claim: Blocking ICOSL has a significant impact on the anti-tumor efficacy of both BI 853520 + anti-OX40 and BI 853520 + anti-4-1BB.
source: Blocking ICOSL had a significant impact on the anti-tumor efficacy of both BI 853520 + anti-OX40 and BI 853520 + anti-4-1BB (Figure 6L,M)
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figures 6L and 6M.

claim: Enhanced T-cell expression of ICOS may be an important mechanism through which a FAK inhibitor can potentiate the anti-tumor activity of anti-OX40 and anti-4-1BB targeted therapies.
source: suggesting that enhanced T-cell expression of ICOS may be an important mechanism through which a FAK inhibitor can potentiate the anti-tumor activity of anti-OX40 and anti-4-1BB targeted therapies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ICOSL blocking experiments.

claim: Anti-GITR alone has no effect on the growth of Panc47 tumors.
source: Anti-GITR alone had no effect on the growth of Panc47 tumors, while in combination with BI 853520 we observed a small growth delay (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Anti-GITR in combination with BI 853520 results in a small growth delay in Panc47 tumors.
source: Anti-GITR alone had no effect on the growth of Panc47 tumors, while in combination with BI 853520 we observed a small growth delay (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Treatment with an anti-CD40 agonistic antibody results in a significant delay in the growth of Panc47 tumors.
source: In contrast, treatment with an anti-CD40 agonistic antibody resulted in a significant delay in the growth of Panc47 tumors, and this was not further enhanced when used in combination with BI 853520 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Anti-CD40 in combination with BI 853520 does not further enhance the growth delay of Panc47 tumors compared to anti-CD40 alone.
source: In contrast, treatment with an anti-CD40 agonistic antibody resulted in a significant delay in the growth of Panc47 tumors, and this was not further enhanced when used in combination with BI 853520 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Treatment of Panc47 tumors with an anti-4-1BB agonistic antibody has no effect on tumor growth.
source: Treatment of Panc47 tumors with an anti-4-1BB agonistic antibody had no effect on tumor growth, but a significant growth delay was observed when used in combination with BI 853520 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Anti-4-1BB in combination with BI 853520 results in a significant growth delay in Panc47 tumors.
source: Treatment of Panc47 tumors with an anti-4-1BB agonistic antibody had no effect on tumor growth, but a significant growth delay was observed when used in combination with BI 853520 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Treatment with an anti-OX40 agonistic antibody has no effect on Panc47 tumor growth.
source: Treatment with an anti-OX40 agonistic antibody had no effect on Panc47 tumor growth, but when used in combination with BI 853520 caused a significant growth delay (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Anti-OX40 in combination with BI 853520 causes a significant growth delay in Panc47 tumors.
source: Treatment with an anti-OX40 agonistic antibody had no effect on Panc47 tumor growth, but when used in combination with BI 853520 caused a significant growth delay (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A FAK kinase inhibitor can render Panc47 tumors sensitive to anti-4-1BB and anti-OX40 immunotherapies.
source: Therefore, a FAK kinase inhibitor can render Panc47 tumors sensitive to anti-4-1BB and anti-OX40 immunotherapies, further supporting the development of these combinations as potential cancer therapies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tumor growth experiments with Panc47 cells.

claim: Gemcitabine treatment of Panc47 tumors results in a significant growth delay that is not further enhanced by combination with either BI 853520 or anti-OX40.
source: Gemcitabine treatment of Panc47 tumors resulted in a significant growth delay that was not further enhanced by combination with either BI 853520 or anti-OX40.
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The triple combination of Gemcitabine + BI 853520 + anti-OX40 improves response when compared to Gemcitabine alone, Gemcitabine + BI 853520, or Gemcitabine + OX40.
source: However, the triple combination of Gemcitabine + BI 853520 + anti-OX40 did improve response when compared to Gemcitabine alone, Gemcitabine + BI 853520, or Gemcitabine + OX40, and tumors were also smaller than corresponding measurements for BI 853520 + anti-OX40 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Gemcitabine exhibits anti-tumor efficacy that can add to that of BI 853520 + anti-OX40.
source: Therefore, Gemcitabine exhibits anti-tumor efficacy that can add to that of BI 853520 + anti-OX40.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the triple combination experiments.

claim: Treatment with a FAK inhibitor can induce potent anti-tumor immune responses in murine models of cancer when used in combination with either endogenous or exogenous signals that promote activation of T-cell co-stimulatory pathways.
source: We show that treatment with a FAK inhibitor can induce potent anti-tumor immune responses in murine models of cancer when used in combination with either endogenous or exogenous signals that promote activation of T-cell co-stimulatory pathways.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: FAK inhibition promotes greater responsiveness to the anti-tumor effects of T-cell co-stimulation through reprogramming multiple immune regulatory pathways.
source: Therefore, FAK inhibition promotes greater responsiveness to the anti-tumor effects of T-cell co-stimulation through reprogramming multiple immune regulatory pathways, supporting further development of these combinations for clinical testing.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanistic findings supported by the immune profiling data.

claim: There is a novel role for FAK in regulating the expression of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L2 on tumor-associated macrophages, monocytic-myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) and cancer cells.
source: Contributing to the enhanced anti-tumor efficacy of these combinations, we identify a novel role for FAK in regulating the expression of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L2 on tumor-associated macrophages, monocytic-myeloid-derived suppressor cells (M-MDSCs) and cancer cells
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing PD-L2 regulation in response to FAK inhibition.

claim: There is a novel role for FAK in regulating expression of the immune co-stimulatory receptor ICOS on effector CD8 T-cells.
source: and in regulating expression of the immune co-stimulatory receptor Inducible T-cell costimulator (ICOS) on effector CD8 T-cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing ICOS regulation in response to FAK inhibition.

claim: CD80 has been linked to promoting anti-tumor immune responses in multiple mouse models of cancer.
source: CD80 has been linked to promoting anti-tumor immune responses in multiple mouse models of cancer (Marchiori et al., 2019; Scarpa et al., 2015; Baskar et al., 1993; Chen et al., 1992; Ganesan et al., 2007; Haile et al., 2011; Hodge et al., 1994; Liu et al., 2001; Townsend and Allison, 1993)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Exogenous administration of recombinant CD80 protein can promote anti-tumor immunity.
source: and exogenous administration of recombinant CD80 protein can promote anti-tumor immunity (Horn et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horn et al., 2018.

claim: Agonistic antibodies and/or RNA aptamers targeting receptors including 4-1BB, OX40, CD40, GITR, ICOS and CD28 are in pre-clinical development and have shown anti-tumor activity in mouse models of cancer.
source: Agonistic antibodies and/or RNA aptamers targeting receptors including 4-1BB, OX40, CD40, GITR, ICOS and CD28 are in pre-clinical development, and have shown anti-tumor activity in mouse models of cancer (Sanmamed et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sanmamed et al., 2015.

claim: A Phase-I clinical trial of the anti-4-1BB antibody PF-05082566 in patients with advanced solid tumors reported an objective response rate of 3.8%.
source: For example, a Phase-I clinical trial of the anti-4-1BB antibody PF-05082566 in patients with advanced solid tumors reported an objective response rate of 3.8% (Segal et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Segal et al., 2018.

claim: MOXR0916 (anti-OX40) achieved stable disease in some patients.
source: while MOXR0916 (anti-OX40) achieved stable disease in some patients (Aaron Hansen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aaron Hansen et al., 2016.

claim: Concurrent administration of anti-PD-1 has been reported to suppress the therapeutic effect of anti-OX40.
source: Concurrent administration of anti-PD-1 has previously been reported to suppress the therapeutic effect of anti-OX40 (Messenheimer et al., 2017; Shrimali et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The suppression of anti-OX40 by anti-PD-1 is likely due to blockade of PD-L1 - PD-1 signaling which is not regulated by FAK.
source: Our findings suggest that these previous observations are likely due to blockade of PD-L1 - PD-1 signaling which is not regulated by FAK.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that FAK regulates PD-L2 but not PD-L1.

claim: The ICOS pathway has previously been implicated in regulating the therapeutic response to anti-OX40, but not 4-1BB.
source: The ICOS pathway has previously been implicated in regulating the therapeutic response to anti-OX40, but not 4-1BB, leading to the conclusion that ICOS signaling on CD4 T-cells was important for anti-OX40 activity (Metzger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Metzger et al., 2016.

claim: ICOS may play an important role in regulating CD8 T-cell responses in some circumstances.
source: Our findings suggest that at least in some circumstances ICOS may also play an important role in regulating CD8 T-cell responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that ICOS blockade impairs both anti-OX40 and anti-4-1BB efficacy.

claim: Ectopic expression of ICOS ligand can result in CD8 T-cell co-stimulation and tumor regression in the absence of CD4 T-cells.
source: Ectopic expression of ICOS ligand can result in CD8 T-cell co-stimulation and tumor regression in the absence of CD4 T-cells (Wallin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wallin et al., 2001.

claim: ICOS-deficient patients have a reduced number of CD8 memory T-cells and impaired CD8 T-cell interferon-γ production.
source: ICOS-deficient patients have a reduced number of CD8 memory T-cells and impaired CD8 T-cell interferon-γ production (Takahashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 2009.

claim: Anti-4-1BB when used in combination with anti-OX40 is more effective at boosting CD8 T-cell expansion, effector function, and anti-tumor immunity.
source: Pre-clinical studies have shown that anti-4-1BB when used in combination with anti-OX40 is more effective at boosting CD8 T-cell expansion, effector function, and anti-tumor immunity (Adler and Vella, 2013; Lee et al., 2004; Morales-Kastresana et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The combination of anti-4-1BB and anti-OX40 has synergistic effects that enhance CD8 T-cell clonal expansion and endow CD8 T-cells with supereffector function.
source: Indeed, this combination is reported to have synergistic effects that not only enhance CD8 T-cell clonal expansion, but also endow CD8 T-cells with supereffector function (Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2007.
